utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed there are no preliminaries. Could that be confirmed by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to put the following on the record in relation to the MFI'd transcripts under number P403. Revised transcripts were submitted by the Prosecution and the Registry may replace the old ones by the new versions of P403, and P403 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Banbury, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, before you give evidence, the Rules require you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banbury. Please be seated. Mr. Banbury, you'll first be examined by Ms. Bibles. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find her to your right. Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Anthony Nathan Banbury.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, what were the dates you were stationed in Bosnia and Herzegovina while working with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: From April 9th, 1994, until May 1st, 1995 in Bosnia. And then later in Zagreb, Croatia, from May 1st, 1995, until November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, is it true that you have provided evidence to the Office of the Prosecutor and have testified before this Tribunal in the Karadzic case with respect to evidence relating to that work?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you provided such evidence in part in the form of a written statement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You first prepared a statement in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And again in 2009?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask to display 65 ter 28667 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, once the document is on the screen I ask that you view this first page, and in particular to look at a signature on that page and indicate whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll now ask that we go to page 53 in e-court of the English version, and I will again ask if you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that's also my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read and review your 2009 statement in preparation for your appearance here today?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 14, which is in e-court on English page 4 and 5 in the B/C/S version, could you review this paragraph and indicate whether there are any corrections that you would like to make to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I would like to point out that in paragraph 14 where it's on the second line where it says "or about 23 April 1993," that should, in fact, say "or about 23 April 1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. With that correction in mind, if the Chamber was to consider your statement will they have an accurate record of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If I were today to ask you questions similar to those you were asked in the taking of this statement, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, the same or substantively the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this statement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, having established the foundational requirements necessary, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear that there are no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28667 receives number P874, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P874 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I read a brief public summary of the witness statement? We have provided copies to the booths and I have explained to the witness the purpose of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Anthony Banbury served with the United Nations in the former Yugoslavia from April 1994 until the end of the conflict. He was first a civil affairs officer in UNPROFOR headquarters in Sarajevo until 1 May 1995. He then worked as an assistant to the special representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Akashi. In both roles, Mr. Banbury attended meetings with leaders of the warring factions and drafted reports, cables, letters, and other correspondence on behalf of his superiors. Mr. Banbury states that the population in Sarajevo suffered because of a constant campaign of shelling and sniping that was directed at civilians. In the course of Mr. Banbury's frequent attendance at meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, Mr. Banbury observed that they were able to modulate the conditions in Sarajevo by controlling the supply of utilities, the freedom of movement, and the level of shelling or sniping, among other things. Your Honours, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, I would ask that we both remember to take pauses between question and answer to allow the translation to catch up. Mr. Banbury, looking at your statement, specifically paragraphs 2 through 4, they summarise your professional biography. I would like to ask just a couple of additional questions. First, was your work with UNPROFOR your first with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No, I had been employed in a few different capacities by the United Nations before I arrived in UNPROFOR. My first position with the United Nations was working as a human rights protection officer on the Thai/Cambodian border in the camps for displaced Cambodians. I spent two years doing that from 1988 to 1990. After that, I worked in the UN peacekeeping operation in Cambodia for about a year and a half as a human rights officer and then briefly in the joint UN organisation of American States OAS mission in Haiti. That mission was expelled from the country until my employment there, and then I moved from there to Bosnia in April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then could you summarise for the Chamber your professional activities since 2009 when you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Shortly after signing this statement I moved from the position I had at the time which was the regional director for Asia of the UN World Food Programme based in Bangkok Thailand where I oversaw operations for that humanitarian organisation throughout Asia. Then in June 2009 I took up my current position as the assistant Secretary-General for field support based at UN headquarters in New York. In that capacity, I -- the deputy in the department of field support where I among -- or, the essential aspect of that work is to provide all kinds of operational support to our peacekeeping and political missions around the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, returning to your time in the former Yugoslavia, could you briefly describe the nature of your two positions while you were there.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: In the first position, the title was civil affairs officer, but my role was not the role of a traditional civil affairs officer. UNPROFOR had civil affairs officers deployed throughout Bosnia and throughout its area of operations in Croatia, et cetera, doing what I would call traditional civil affairs work, working with local communities, et cetera. I was, essentially, a political affairs officer working for the delegate of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, the DSRSG, Mr. Viktor Andreev initially, later Mr. Enrique Aguilar. In that capacity I went along with him to meetings on an almost daily basis, meetings of all kinds with warring factions, with diplomatic community, with other UN entities, internal meetings of UNPROFOR with, say, his military counterpart, initially General Rose, later General Smith. And then depending on the nature of the meeting, certainly if it was a meeting with an external party, I would then write a report to normally UNPROFOR headquarters in which I sought to summarise what had actually happened in the meeting, a factual accounting of what transpired. And then normally at the end of the document include some kind of analysis of the significance of the conversation, the next steps that perhaps we needed to take, the issues at stake, trying to help our superiors in Zagreb understand the significance of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in the meetings if you were part of a meeting and you were working with or meeting with individuals from the Bosnian government side, who from that side was typically also attending the meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The officials on the Bosnian government side with whom I had the most contact were President Izetbegovic, Prime Minister Salajdzic, Vice-President Ganic, and Minister Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Then when you attended meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, could you describe who attended those meetings from the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The officials on the Bosnian Serb side with whom I had the most contact were Dr. Karadzic, Professor Koljevic, General Mladic, General Gvero, General Tolimir, and Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Krajisnik. At times Mr. Zametica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Then when you moved to your second position based out of Zagreb, who did you meet with predominantly in the meetings after that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I took up my new position as a special assistant to the SRSG on May 1 1995, based in Zagreb. I had very similar duties and responsibilities, but in that case for the SRSG as opposed to for his delegate in Bosnia. And there, of course, given the nature of my superior's responsibilities, instead of focusing just on Bosnia we also worked a lot with authorities in Zagreb, in Croatia, and in Serbia, in Belgrade. And there the main officials were President Tudjman and President Milosevic, also Mr. Sarinic on the Croatian side, sometimes General Perisic on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In addition to these meetings, what other sources of information did you rely upon in preparing your reports and assessments?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I, for the most part, wrote two kinds of reports. One were -- one set was on the meetings that I attended, and there was just what happened in those meetings plus the analysis at the end. I also, though, routinely wrote a weekly report that sought to summarise -- when I was in Bosnia, when I was in Bosnia -- that sought to summarise the events of the week, what had happened in the week, and the meaning of it. And that was a report that I would prepare but Mr. Andreev would sign. It would come from him to our headquarters in Zagreb. And there, myself, or other colleagues when they wrote it, sought to draw on whatever information sources we could find. It was a wide range. We had regular contacts with the diplomatic community, with humanitarian community. We rely quite heavily on the local press from all sides, the Bosniak, Croat, Serb side. We had some very good national staff who monitored the press very closely, the radio, TV, newspaper, and would provide us with an analysis of the key developments in the press or key reports in the press. And we would often use those. So we were able to, I think, develop a fairly good picture -- oh, we also relied very heavily from UNPROFOR reports from the field, our civil affairs officers, our UN military observers, military contingents deployed in the field, they were deployed throughout Bosnia, and we -- they all submitted weekly reports. And that combination of UNPROFOR reporting, formal and informal engagement with the diplomatic community, meetings with the parties themselves, local press reporting, that combination gave us a pretty good picture, I think, of what was happening, and we sought to -- or, I sought to distill that in my weekly reports to the most important developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During your time in the former Yugoslavia, did you have a sense as to the gravity of the events that you were witnessing in these meetings in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It was a coincidence, but it nonetheless had a big impact on me. I was deployed to Bosnia on April 9th, 1994, right at the peak or almost peak of the Gorazde crisis. And I got off the plane and went to my new headquarters and there was all this talk about use of NATO air power, blue sword as they called it, and generals running around. And the day after was the first use of NATO air power in the history of the organisation. So from literally the first hours I was in the country, I had the sense that these were important things that were happening. Of course I read the press and was familiar with the war from an outside perspective, but upon arriving and, really, every day that I was there I felt like we all were living history for better or worse. And I had that sense really in two important ways. One was the humanitarian or human impact of what was happening, just seeing how people's lives were affected; you saw that every day. And the -- it couldn't help but have a huge impact on how you saw people living on any side of any line. You could tell that real human beings were suffering terribly. Societies were being riven apart, families riven apart, communities destroyed. The other -- the other main way that I really felt history was being made was because decisions that were being taken by people I was working with on a daily basis, either people in the United Nations or officials of the different parties, those decisions were history in the making. Those decisions, you know, have -- used NATO air power, not use NATO air power, let UN flights land or not let UN flights, let a convoy go to Gorazde or not let a convoy go to Gorazde, these things had a huge, huge, huge impact on people's lives, and sometimes they were life-and-death questions. They were peace-and-war questions. And you -- certainly myself working in Bosnia-Herzegovina command headquarters had the sense every day that history was being made.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: How did that awareness impact your efforts to observe and preserve the events as they happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I felt like I had a very important and in some ways privileged responsibility because of the assignment that was given to me. Normally when a civil affairs officer was first deployed to Bosnia, a newcomer like myself, he or she would be sent out to one of the regional offices, spend a year out in a place like Gorazde or Gornji Vakuf or somewhere like that. But for whatever reason, Mr. Andreev from the day I arrived kind of attached me to his personal office, and so I was privileged in that sense but also privileged to be watching this history and a witness to the history in the making and that created a -- I think, a very big responsibility on me and the position I was given to try and be a faithful recorder of it. And as a result, I tried very hard to transcribe the events as they were happening. In the notes I took I tried very hard to reflect accurately what he said, what she said, what he said. And then, you know, try and provide that information to our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you observe and note the negotiating practices and strategies of the various parties?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I sat in dozens and dozens and dozen of meetings with officials and often the most senior officials of the different sides. And as a result, I was able to observe, yes, their negotiating approaches to important issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the negotiating style of Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think General Mladic was or is a very intelligent, strategic thinker. I was always very impressed by General Mladic, his grasp of the issues, his strategic approach to the issues. I thought he was one of the more intelligent and strategically minded actors of the ones that I was exposed to on any of the sides, including the UN. He was very effective in meetings, using a combination of, I would, say charm and almost bullying, where you had the choice of either kind of going along with the charm offensive and his points and his sides and that would, you know, be very easy and comfortable and a much more pleasant experience, or resisting it and opposing him, and that would lead to a less enjoyable experience. And he was, I would say, a very negotiator.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you able to discern any particular techniques and strategies employed by Mladic, particularly with respect to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The main strategy that I discerned on the Bosnian Serb side, and it was apparent early for me even in the Gorazde crisis but became more pronounced over time, was on the critical issue of the use of force by the UN and NATO. And I think it was clear that the Bosnian Serbs did not want to have the UN or NATO use force against them. They didn't want another combatant warring against them. And the way I believe General Mladic sought to achieve his objective of keeping us at bay was to -- whenever the UN was inclined to use force or did use force, particularly NATO air power, he would ensure through process of escalation that the Bosnian Serbs at the end of that crisis were in a superior position to the United Nations and that we were in a much worse position than when we started. And this pattern was repeated across a number of occasions when we used NATO air power. And the way they ensured that was by doing things like shutting down the airport which was critical to us, blocking our movement so we could not resupply our troops in the enclaves, blocking humanitarian convoys, taking hostages at times, refusing to negotiate. So in each use of our -- each time we used force we ended up in a worse position and that had both a big operational impact on the United Nations but it also had a big, I think, psychological impact on certain UN officials in UNPROFOR but also in UN government officials well beyond the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, I noticed that you at various occasions by your faces, by the way in which you seek communication with other persons in this courtroom, including me, that you in some way react and respond to what the witness says. And you are hereby instructed not to do it any further because you know what the consequences are if you continue to express any feeling or thoughts even without words about the testimony of a witness. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You testified that your first day was the beginning of the first NATO air strikes in Gorazde. And in your statement just roughly paragraphs 10 through 22 you describe both the circumstances on the ground and also the negotiating position of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Focusing on that time-period in April and May of 1994, how did the Bosnian Serb actions with respect to Gorazde influence peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Gorazde was a very serious political, humanitarian, and military crisis for UNPROFOR and the people of Gorazde, and the use by NATO of air power for the first time, the shooting down of a British aircraft by the Bosnian Serbs, the killing of some British soldiers in Gorazde, this created not only a major crisis for the United Nations and -- it forced us to reflect very seriously on our role in the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia, in -- on our relationship with the Bosnian Serbs. And I think the Bosnian Serb leadership, including very much General Mladic, saw the weakness -- weaknesses of the UN, understood clearly our vulnerabilities - in this, by "vulnerabilities" I'm talking about the political will to pursue more forceful course of action - and were very smart in exploiting the UN's weaknesses and vulnerabilities. They did it through a combination of use of force and measures that I think speak for themselves in terms of what they did to the United Nations, but also in the meetings and discussions that we had, they realised they had a superior position. They staked out very hard-line positions and demands in the negotiations, very inflexible, and were able to quite effectively use -- well, first develop leverage over us and then use that leverage to achieve their -- or at least advance their objectives in the Gorazde area but also very much in terms of the strategic relationship between the Bosnian Serbs and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention now to paragraph 19 which in e-court the English version would be page 6 and in B/C/S, page 7. In paragraph 19 you state that: "By attaching unreasonable conditions to their offer of peace, they were perpetuating the war." Could you describe for us what those conditions were that the Bosnian Serb leadership was asking?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: In this particular context they were referring to a per cent of land that would be allocated to the Bosnian Serbs in a potential peace agreement. They were referring to the width of a corridor in northern Bosnia linking western and eastern Bosnia, the Posavina corridor around Brcko. They were referring to access to the sea. And while it's normal in negotiations to perhaps stake out a position that you're willing to, you know, make compromises from, I don't believe that was the case here, in part because this was a very common tactic that the Bosnian Serb leadership used throughout the war, the civilian and military leadership where they would say one thing, whether it's they wanted peace or they wanted to have a POW exchange or they wanted to have utilities flowing in Sarajevo, but their actions made clear that they in fact were pursuing a very different objective. And we -- we saw that -- I saw that time and time again, where they staked out entirely unreasonable positions and then placed the burden on the UN to get their counterparts, the Bosniaks, the Croats, to make the concessions necessary to achieve these very unattainable positions and it left the UN in a very difficult position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, well if not for the full hundred per cent then at least for 90 per cent this is perfectly clear from the statement. Of course you ask now the witness to again state about the corridor or the 50 per cent of land. This is a 92 ter witness with a lengthy statement. Would you please try to avoid repetitious evidence and put such questions that really add something to what we have already in the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Pulling back to the big picture, from April to September of 1994 could you describe politically and in terms of military terms what effect those developing patterns had on the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The -- in the wake of the Gorazde crisis, there was a strong diplomatic push by external actors leading to the so-called Geneva Agreement from I think it was June, and that led to an improvement in the climate in Bosnia, but as was often the case when there was some kind of political agreement it didn't last very long. The political agreement was more a result of external pressures rather than any of the parties involved fundamentally reassessing and changing their war aims and their fundamental interests. And while things improved in June and July, by August they were deteriorating and the political process was more or less in shambles and the military developments were getting -- were becoming more predominant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In terms of the international or even within the former Yugoslavia, in terms of the support that the Bosnian Serb leadership had in their relationship with these other entities, by September of 1994 were those relationships stronger or had they started to dissolve?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Sorry, the relationship with which entities?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With the leadership in Pale and other entities in both the former Yugoslavia and internationally.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think there was a gradual move towards isolation of the Bosnian Serbs. They were over time losing support of key actors who weren't necessarily their allies but were reliable supporters and that support was weakening. And whether it was in Moscow or in Belgrade or, to some extent, Paris and London, we saw I think more and more external actors perceive the Bosnian Serb position to be an unreasonable one and didn't want to be associated with it and wanted them to move toward a more reasonable one that could produce a peace agreement or a cease-fire or a calming of the situation. And there was a perception that the Bosnian Serbs were making that goal very difficult to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, may I invite you to read with me your last question. You were talking about "the support that the Bosnian Serb leadership had in their relationship with these and other entities," and then you were asked "relationship with which entities?" And then you said "with the leadership in Pale and other entities." So you are asking a question about the relationship between the Bosnian Serb leadership had with the leadership in Pale. It is really confusing me quite a bit and I would prefer that you are clear in your questions and perhaps asking this witness of facts -- primarily his knowledge of facts because you are at this moment eliciting political analysis, assessment of situations, not to say that it is not relevant and that we wouldn't like to hear it, but if it becomes that vague that you are asking about the relationship the Pale leadership had with itself then it's time to think about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'll attempt to be more articulate as to the parties I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, moving to the fall of 1994, were there areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina which were particularly reliant on the aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes. There was of course a large number of people throughout Bosnia on all sides dependent on humanitarian assistance, but the ones most dependent were the ones in the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia and to an extent in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What was your understanding as to the United Nations -- as to whether the United Nations was to be permitted freedom of movement with respect to these areas?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The Security Council made very clear in its resolutions that the United Nations was to be given full freedom of movement to carry out its responsibilities. Initially those responsibilities were very heavily focused on humanitarian assistance, Resolution 776 and others; that evolved over time to include other things. But it was clear that one of the very fundamental roles of UNPROFOR was to support the delivery of humanitarian assistance to civilians in need and that we were to be accorded freedom of movement by all parties to achieve that objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you describe whether there was actual freedom of movement to these areas in the fall of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The United Nations never had what I would -- or UNPROFOR never had what I would call freedom of movement in Bosnia. We were constantly impeded in our movements, whether it was for delivery of humanitarian assistance or other activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've described some of these specifics in your statement but could you tell us whether you were able to determine whether these restrictions were based on local action or whether it was coming from a higher place in the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The subject of freedom of movement was very often discussed by the leadership of UNPROFOR with their interlocutors on the Bosnian Serb side, with Dr. Karadzic and his colleagues on the civilian side; with General Mladic and his colleagues on the military side. We discussed it again and again and again. They were acutely aware of their responsibilities under the Security Council mandate. They were acutely aware of the fact that they were failing to fulfil these responsibilities. And despite the repeated requests from Mr. Akashi on down, they refused to accord us the freedom of movement we needed and had the right to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In drafting letters to the various players in the former Yugoslavia with respect to these restrictions, were you cognisant of the particular tenor or tone that those letters would take with respect to the events which they were describing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR always sought to be very respectful to all parties and accord the leadership of the parties the respect that we felt was due to them, but we also put a higher priority on implementation of our mandate and our responsibilities toward the people, all the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we had to try and strike a difficult balance, whether it was in letters or in meetings, between on the one hand maintaining cordial, respectful relations, and on the other really focusing on getting our job done.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 78 you described drafting a letter from Mr. Andreev to Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could I ask you, in drafting a letter you would say that the drafter could be not cognisant of the tone which is adopted in that letter? Is that -- because that's what -- was your question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I was eliciting an explanation as to the recognition of the different types of -- or the elevation in tone and tenor with respect to certain incidents to put the next document in context, Your Honour, perhaps not artfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you were asking is whether as a drafter the witness was cognisant of the tone in which certain events were described in the text he drafted. Now, I have some difficulties in understanding if you draft a document that you would not know about the tone you are using. I mean, that's the privilege of the drafter I would say. Therefore, could you please come to relevant, concrete points as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could bring 65 ter 10586 to the screen, please, specifically the second page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the -- in diplomatic terms the tenor that was used in this particular letter, that you used in this particular letter?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This was a letter in which we, I guess, used very direct, explicit language. Mr. Andreev was someone who I think generally sought to understand the perspectives of all parties to the conflict. As a Russian I think he had a particular ability to understand the perspective of the Serbs and establish generally positive relationships with the Bosnian Serb authorities, which was a good thing. So he had a particular role and could play a role different than some other UN officials could. Given how serious the situation was in Bosnia at the time of the writing of this letter, in part following the Bihac crisis in late November 1994, I thought it was critical or at least appropriate for Mr. Andreev to use extremely direct, frank language with Dr. Karadzic so there could be no misunderstanding at all about how grave the situation was, about the responsibilities the Bosnian Serb leadership had for its part -- they weren't the only ones responsible, but they had a responsibility for getting the situation to where it was, and the implications of their behaviour and what might follow if they -- if they did not change it so there could be no misunderstanding later on if -- if things happened a certain way as to them not having been put on notice of what was -- what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 10586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10586 receives number P875, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P875 is admitted. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 75, your statement describes a meeting between General Rose and others regarding NATO's position in Bosnia. I note that this is an example where General Mladic is not actually present in the meeting. Was it your experience in these negotiations that an agreement could have been reached without General Mladic's authorisation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: In my experience, any significant decision or agreement -- decision by the Bosnian Serbs that had military implications or agreement with the Bosnian Serbs that had military implications could only be reached with the consent of General Mladic. There were many conversations, discussions, negotiations that took place without him present, and that meant one of two things: Either the issues being discussed were of -- not of a level that required his engagement or that the decision or agreement wasn't going to be reached in that room and needed to be referred to him or he had already given his consent to a certain position. And I think that was -- that was pretty clear to me over time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Moving to the end of 1994, could you describe for us briefly whether you were involved in the negotiations for the 31st December 1994 cessation of hostilities agreement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I was assigned by the SRSG to President Carter as the UNPROFOR political advisor notetaker for his negotiations. So I was the only UN person attached to President Carter's delegation and was present with him for all his meetings with the different parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us whether Mladic was actively involved in these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: General -- for President Carter's negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs, General Mladic was normally present, but I would not say he was actively involved in the formal meetings. I, of course, don't know what role, if any, he played behind the scenes, but in terms of the discussions with President Carter, those were generally led by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Moving on now to the spring of 1995, starting in -- around paragraph 92 you indicate that this agreement started to break down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we see 65 ter 10592 on our screens. And for reference, this is referred to in paragraphs 93 and 94. And if we could go to e-court page 3 in English and 6 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like you -- to direct your attention to paragraph 7, where it reads: "The increasingly clear intention of the BSA appears to be to permit delivery of supplies to the enclaves necessary for our survival, but not those needed in order for us to function." Was this level of control of freedom of movement a new point in terms of negotiations, which you've described as negotiations, with the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was a new point. It was used across the time-span of the conflict as a very powerful source of leverage over the UN. What was perhaps a little bit new or evolving around this time was what I assessed to be the Bosnian Serbs' decision to really find a way to neutralise the UN and neutralise our ability to act in Eastern Bosnia by drastically limiting our ability to supply our personnel and deliver humanitarian assistance. And I think there were two main objectives there. There was the operational one by limiting the delivery of, say, food and fuel to our troops. Our troops sometimes had to sleep in unheated accommodation, they had to patrol on mules, they had to do foot patrols, they couldn't run generators, so that limited our operational ability to work. But there was also a very important psychological impact, I think, on the UNPROFOR -- on some UNPROFOR leaders, both in Eastern Bosnia and in Sarajevo as well as in Zagreb, where we became dependent upon the Serbs to function, for us to function for us to live. And very often the Bosnian Serb leadership, General Mladic and others, would say: If -- we're doing this because the Bosnian government is, you know, using an enclave for military purposes or one thing or another, so you need to go get the Bosnian government to change its behaviour. And if you do that, then we'll give you the ability to resupply yourselves. So we got into the position of supplicant to the Pale leadership, kind of beseeching them, please let us have food and fuel, and some folks got -- ended up blaming the Bosnian government for our plight in the enclaves. I think this was particularly true of some of the leaders in the enclaves or some of the enclaves, and it was -- it was a very intelligent, well-crafted strategy on the part of the Bosnian Serbs because it totally reversed the situation where we wanted to get -- we wanted to make the Bosnian Serbs happy and make them like us and we were very angry - by "we" I mean some of the UN officials - angry at the Bosnian government because of all these restrictions placed on UNPROFOR by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break. We already can allow the witness to leave the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. Ms. Bibles, apart from that, are you on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Very much, Your Honour. A little ahead of schedule actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would mean that you would need how much time after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: About 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About 15 minutes. We'll then resume at five minutes to 11.00 and you'll finish by ten minutes past. We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although briefly, we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll take this opportunity to tender the document we were looking at, 65 ter 10592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10592 receives number P876, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P876 is admitted into evidence. You needed another 15 minutes? You may proceed as soon as the witness has taken his seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be considerably shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, I'd like to direct your attention to paragraphs 94 and 95 of your statement. And I should note, Mr. Banbury has a copy of his statement in front of him. In paragraph 94 you report a statement made by General Mladic to General Smith: "'The increase in sniping by the Bosnian Serb army in the Sarajevo area was in response to Serb casualties suffered in military offensives launched by the Bosnian government ...'" In paragraph 95 of your statement you indicate that you understood Mladic to be referring to the sniping of civilians. Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The victims of sniping in Sarajevo were predominantly, the vast majority, were civilians. Sniping is not an indiscriminate use of force where the victims are, you know, just in the wrong places at the wrong time. The sniper chooses very specifically their victim and the victims of sniping in Sarajevo were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Finally, early in your testimony you described that you understood one of the important aspects of what you were observing had to do with the human impact. What did you observe during the time you were in the former Yugoslavia as the human impact of Ratko Mladic's actions in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: For a UN person, for someone -- for any person, I think, to see the impact of the war in Bosnia was -- was very -- it was very difficult. There were civilians who were being killed, who were being displaced, who -- families being broken up, terrible crimes committed against women, and this was going on around us every day, those of us working in UNPROFOR. And one -- I don't think UN people showed up -- certainly I didn't show up in UNPROFOR thinking that this side is right or that side is wrong. We weren't there to help one side or hurt another side. We were there to help civilians and minimise the impact of this terrible war, but unfortunately the consequences of the war for civilians just grew over time. And whether it's a, you know, young -- it doesn't matter the nationality of the young child or old mother who gets, you know, shot and killed, the Bosnian -- I lived in Sarajevo for 15 months and -- during the war and what the Bosnian Serb army did to the population of that city, whoever they were, Bosniaks, Croats, Serbs, was -- you know, they terrorised the city. People didn't know if they walked out their door if they were going to come back, or if a mother sent their kids out a door if the kids would come back or the father would come back or their grandmother. Someone walking around Sarajevo in the period I was there could be killed any time. Whether it was by a sniper's bullet or a mortar fired indiscriminately into the city, people could be killed any time. And that had not only a huge, you know, humanitarian impact, lots of people were killed, but the psychological impact on the population of the city was I think devastating. I had a lot of, you know, Bosnian friends and they -- their families suffered so much, certainly because they were freezing cold, they didn't have electricity, they didn't have gas, they didn't have food, but much worse than those kinds of deprivations was the terror they felt from living in a city not only under siege but where civilians were being routinely killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could I ask you -- your last question was what the witness observed about the human impact of Ratko Mladic's actions in Bosnia. The answer was about the impact of the war and, in a later part of the answer, the impact of the acts of the Bosnian Serb army. The witness didn't say a word about Mr. Mladic. I would like to have clarified whether he understood all the war misery to be directly attributed to Mr. Mladic or perhaps only the acts of the Bosnian Serb army because that was your question. Now, could you clarify your answer as to whether it was about Ratko Mladic's actions or about the war and the activities of the Bosnian Serb army that you told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I apologise for not being more precise in my answer in response to the question. The -- certainly the misery endured by the civilians, whether in Sarajevo or elsewhere in Bosnia, was the result of many factors that went well beyond just the actions of the Bosnian Serb army or certainly General Mladic. However, the -- there is no question in my mind and based on my direct experience that there -- for the people of Sarajevo but also the people of Gorazde and Zepa and Bihac and Srebrenica and Tuzla and many other cities in Bosnia, civilians living in them, that the Bosnian Serb army terrorised them physically and psychologically. And there is, likewise, no doubt in my mind based on my observations that General Mladic was the undisputed leader of the Bosnian Serb army who made the decisions and gave the orders and his orders were followed. And the Bosnian Serb army did what it was told to do by its leadership. And that the plight of civilians in Sarajevo during the period I was there was rendered almost unbearable by the actions of the Bosnian Serb army that were directed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge also has a question or questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I may, I have a follow-up question to that, what you just told us. During the meetings when you met General Mladic, did you raise and did you express your concerns about your observations -- about the impact these actions had on the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, normally in meetings I did not speak much. I was a junior officer and was there essentially as a notetaker. To some degree over time and later on in my time there I would speak up on occasion. But normally it was my superiors who were conducting the negotiations and discussions. But I certainly witnessed my superiors on the civilian and the military side raise on countless occasions with General Mladic, with Dr. Karadzic, with their colleagues, the deep concern we had for the impact of their actions, their decisions, the Bosnian Serb army on the civilians, whether it was civilian deaths caused by sniping or mortar fire or the humanitarian impact on people by blocking delivery of humanitarian supplies. We did the same thing with the other sides when their actions created a negative impact on the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall the reaction of General Mladic during such meetings when this issue was raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was raised so many times, but normally there was some combination of either blaming the other side for whatever the action was or in linking, as in the recent example just cited, Bosnian Serb action to something unrelated; so sniping civilians in Sarajevo because of Serb casualties on a front line somewhere else. So there was some effort to justify the behaviour or there was a denial of it or an expression of not being aware of it and a pledge to investigate, which I never found very credible, or to minimise the particular incident that was being raised. So it was normally some combination of those, justifying, denying or pledging to investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be questioned by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I assume that you have your statement before you.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and go through certain parts of your statement. If I have understood you correctly, you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina one day after your 30th birthday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that you were a fairly young man who had an extremely difficult job to do and a lot of responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you been trained in any way with regard to what you were to expect in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April 1994? Had you been briefed? Had you learned anything about the situation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I had, I think, very relevant and significant experience with the United Nations in conflict and post conflict zones before my arrival in Bosnia that enabled me to carry out my job. In terms of my briefing on the actual conflict in Bosnia, I had the normal induction briefing of UN personnel when I arrived in Zagreb a few days before I arrived in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And P874, if we could have it on the screen, please, paragraph 5, and also in the course of the examination-in-chief today you mentioned the manner in which you understood the task you had to carry out. What I would like you to explain to us today is the following, it concerns paragraph 5 in the English version, Your Honours -- in the English version, Your Honours, it will be on the following page. You said, amongst other things, that your mission was also to interpret UNPROFOR's mandate for colleagues who held official, or rather, military posts, especially this was for the benefit of the commander Michael Rose, the commander of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and commander Rupert Smith. Would you tell the Court in what way you carried out this mandate of -- or in what way you carried out this task of interpreting UNPROFOR's mandate?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It started with a serious study of resolutions that had been adopted by the UN Security Council with respect to UNPROFOR's mandate; and then based on that study - I have a degree in international law which helped me in my analysis of those resolutions - then trying to explain to my superiors on the civilian side but also the senior military officers what the meaning of that or the resolutions were in a given context. Very often the interpretation was contextual following -- you know, in the Gorazde crisis, what was our responsibility? What were we obligated to do? What were we authorised to do? But it was up to the leaders to decide what to do because they were not necessarily obligated to do something; they perhaps only had the authorisation to. So it was mainly in that way that I sought to help them understand either their responsibilities or at least the authorities they had if they chose to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But would we agree that there were various ways in which UNPROFOR's mandate was interpreted or viewed and members of UNPROFOR themselves viewed it in different ways; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct. Unfortunately, for various reasons, the Security Council Resolutions had a degree of ambiguity in them that left them open to interpretation and different interpretations. And so it was sometimes a challenging task because the military wanted something very clear and definitive and we were not always able to give them a clear, definitive answer to their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to these various interpretations of UNPROFOR's mandate in various crisis situations that you were involved in, these interpretations kept reoccurring in the field; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now have a look at paragraph 11 in your statement. P874. And could we see the document in e-court, 65 ter document 10641. Sir, in paragraph 11 you refer to this document, in fact, and in response to a question put to you by the Prosecution you comment on it. I would like to clarify certain issues in that paragraph now. If I have understood this correctly, this telegram or this document was drafted by three authors; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Dejan Mihov, David Harland, and yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because I would like to focus on paragraph 4 in this document, paragraph 4 in the B/C/S version, and in the English version it's on the next page, Your Honours. This was mentioned in paragraph 11 of the witness's statement. So the first thing I would like to ask you about is whether you can remember of the three of you, who, in fact, drafted this report or message dated the 18th of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I believe that all three of us had a role in drafting the document, which probably meant some of us wrote some paragraphs, some wrote the other, but in the end we all reviewed it and had a chance to make comments on the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So that would also be your point of view in relation to what it says in paragraph 4, that is the text that should be provided?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, it's likely that one of the three of us wrote paragraph 4 but that all three of us in reviewing the entire document had a chance to review that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it states, among other things, that in the event of people leaving Gorazde en masse in Sarajevo, other areas under the control of the government of the ABiH, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would become more radical and the conflict would probably continue. You said what you thought about that, and in the light of what you said in paragraph 11 of your statement my question is as follows: On the basis of what experience did you draw the conclusion that this would be one of the main obstacles to peace? And this is what you stated in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think it's unlikely that I was the drafter of paragraph 4. I think it was more likely one of other two colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that Mr. Harland drafted it, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I don't know which of the three of us drafted it. I'm sorry, I don't recall. My guess is it was more likely to be Mr. Mihov, but if you told me that Mr. Harland did it I could certainly believe that's a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not making that claim, but I'm asking you about this because I want to know whether they would allow you to comment in paragraph 11 on something that someone else wrote, not yourself, one of the three of you but not yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. I apologise. You are commenting on what paragraph 4 was supposed to mean. In paragraph 11 of your statement, I just want you to confirm something, in fact, that you are commenting on the text drafted by someone else. And this is, in fact, the way in which you interpret something that someone else drafted. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And given that this is your interpretation, what is the opinion of the three of you in paragraph 4 when you say that this situation, the influence of the military units of the ABiH is composed of displaced persons from Eastern Bosnia would be one of the main obstacles to peace?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I can only speak for myself and not the colleagues at the time, but it is my understanding that our -- we assess that where there was serious displacement of population, where there was so-called ethnic cleansing, violent displacement of people, burning of homes perhaps, terrible crimes committed against women, that this would -- on any side, this would quite naturally make the survivors, the families, you know, very hostile to the party that carried out these acts and deeply opposed to any kind of reconciliation with them, perhaps seeking, you know, if not revenge at least victory over the other side and less inclined to compromise. And so for in this particular case the people in the communities and units made up of people who were displaced through violence from Eastern Bosnia, those people would be less inclined to compromise with the party that they assigned responsibility to for these acts than, say, people who had not been so directly a victim of violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly why I asked you this. Now, based on your experience during your stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you say that both sides ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you just restart your question. You said, "Based on your experience during your stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina would you say ..." and then continue your question from there on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you say then that this pattern of taking revenge because of something that someone had gone through would have been something that would affect both warring parties?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: As a general matter, I think it is human nature and it's -- in the case of Bosnia it's all three parties, I think, human nature if you see something terrible or horrible done to a family member, your neighbour, that you are then angry, upset, want revenge or victory over the people. You want justice against the people who have carried that out. And I think this is a human reaction that applied to civilians, people, or military, for that matter, in all parties in the conflict in Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at paragraph 6 of this message, this document, that we have before us which reads: "The situation -- the unstable situation persists. Bosnian infantry, released from Sarajevo by the TEZ, is destabilising the main western confrontation line and the Nisici plateau ..." Now, my question is this: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what you meant by the words "Bosnian infantry released from Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, again, it's not necessarily the case that I drafted that paragraph, but I think the meaning of it is that because of the agreement or the requirement by the Security Council and the UN on the total exclusion zone around Sarajevo, that led to a lessening of conflict in that area; and as a result the parties were able to redirect military assets that they had previously concentrated in the Sarajevo area to other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's take a look at paragraph 10 of this document where it says: "The Council must clarify the concept of the Safe Areas as soon as possible ..." And then you go on to explain what that implies. So my question for you is this: Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether at any point in time the UNPROFOR mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina received an official explanation from the council describing the exact meaning of the concept of safe areas or whether this issue and the various perception of what the term "safe area" implies remained open throughout your stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina, unresolved in other words?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The only explanation or guidance that UNPROFOR received from the Security Council on the safe areas was in the form of its official documents, resolutions, presidential statements, and in particularly -- in particular Resolutions 824 and 836. So we did not get guidance beyond that from the Security Council and UNPROFOR was left to interpret the resolutions and its responsibilities largely on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'll put a very specific question to you: Would I be correct if I said that such different approaches to the concept of safe areas did not have an answer to the question of whether UNPROFOR, and I quote, "should tolerate the fact that the Bosnian army used them, took advantage of them, for military purpose"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The two primary Security Council Resolutions dealing with safe areas did not create an obligation on the Bosnian government forces to withdraw from the safe areas. And in fact in 836 there was an explicit requirement of the Bosnian Serb forces and related militia to withdraw from the safe areas -- to a safe distance from the safe areas. And by specifically creating that obligation on the Bosnian Serb forces while remaining silent on the Bosnian government forces, it was the interpretation of myself and, I think, several others that there was thus no requirement for the Bosnian government forces to withdraw their military from the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that there were different interpretations about the Bosnian army in the safe areas, the enclaves, that, in fact, should be disarmed and that that was, after all, the mandate that UNPROFOR had?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: There were different views within UNPROFOR and beyond about the -- what should be the role of the Bosnian military, if any, whether there should be a presence or not in the safe areas. For the most part those difference of views were not based on different interpretations of Security Council Resolutions and obligations imposed by those resolutions; rather, the difference of views was a result of an assessment that the continued -- an assessment by some that the continued presence of Bosnian government forces in the safe areas was a destabilising factor and creating problems and it would be better if the Bosnian government forces either were not there or were not active in the safe areas. But that was more on an operational assessment as opposed to an interpretation of a legal obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If we accepted the interpretation according to which the BH army would not have the duty to demilitarise within the safe areas and that it may remain as an organised and armed force and launch attacks out of the safe areas, would that mean, according to you as you've just explained, that the VRS, the Army of the Bosnian Serbs, would not have the right to counter such attacks because of its obligation under Resolution 876 of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It is clear, I think, from Resolution 824 and 836 that there was a clear, unambiguous obligation on the Bosnian Serb army and any other force not to attack the six safe areas. There was no provision that allowed them to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you agree with me then that such a difference in positions caused continuous problems in all the talks with the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's just briefly take a look at paragraph 11 of this document and then we will be done with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, paragraph 11, that's on the next page in both the B/C/S and English versions. It's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it reads: "UNPROFOR's mandate has pushed it into low-level conflict with the Serbs ..." And you say: "Our mandate must either be one within which we are able to have a co-operative relationship with the Serbs, or it must be one in which we have the force to impose our will. It cannot be - as it is now - somewhere in between." You talked about this in paragraph 12 of your statement, and we have that statement before us so I won't repeat myself. But let me ask you just this: At any point in time while you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina - and I'm not referring to you personally, sir - were you ever given a different interpretation of the UNPROFOR mandate as opposed to the time when this -- when this telegram was drafted?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No, not fundamentally. There were some additional capabilities assigned to UNPROFOR, but the fundamental mandate was never changed so that ambiguity remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And we can agree that this was a constant cause, as you stated here, of a low-level intensity -- low-level conflict with the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I don't believe that UNPROFOR was engaged in a constant conflict with the Bosnian Serbs, at least -- certainly not militarily. That came and went for very brief periods, but for the most part we were not engaged in any kind of military conflict with the Serbs except in those short periods. The -- it did create political tensions between the Bosnian Serbs and UNPROFOR, though, throughout that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then just one final question which I hear from what you've said. You said that some points in time UNPROFOR was in conflict with the Serbs. Can we agree that in some periods that conflict was a high-intensity conflict, where it was necessary to use very strong resources of the NATO Pact?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, with the slight qualification that very strong resources of NATO were used. Whether it was necessary or not I think is a matter of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mention in your statement and I will talk about this a little later, but did you see this conflict as a situation where UNPROFOR, in fact, was a warring party and that its opponent was the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence. It is on our -- actually, it's on the OTP 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10641 receives number D186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D186 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will return to paragraphs 17 and 18 of your statement, but for now let's take a look at para 24 where you were shown a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, could we pull up this document in e-court? That's 09738, 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you discuss this document in paragraph 24 of your statement and I would just like to remind you that you also discussed this document in the Karadzic case. Now having reminded you of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we now see 1D00708 in e-court. 1D00708.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that you had occasion to see this document. You were shown it in the Karadzic case. And if you need some time to go through it, please let us know, but I will just have a few questions about this and the interpretation of the document that we saw a little earlier. This is a document sent from a forward command post, an IKM, from the VKRS. And in paragraph 1 it says: "On the 27th of April, 1994 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Your Honour, we should just see who the author of this document is and then we can go back to this page. With your leave, could we see the last page first because that will give us the full context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So we see the document was signed by Major-General Milan Gvero. Thank you. And now could we go back to page 1, please. It says here, sir, that on the 27th of April, 1994, at a joint meeting of representatives of the VKRS - and in a moment I'll ask you to assist us with interpreting this VKRS - and the UN representative, Mr. De Mello, and General Soubirou, it was stated that the Gorazde cease-fire agreement was reached, the agreement between Mr. Akashi and President Karadzic had been implemented in its entirety in accordance with the agreed -- what had been agreed and the resolution. Then in paragraph 3 it says: "It was agreed that VRS soldiers in the stated sectors," in other words in a 3-kilometre-wide zone, "will put on civilian clothes with the explanation that these are villagers that do not have any other clothes since their village was burned down by the Muslims. It was also agreed that some local police officers will put on civilian clothes and that all the problems with UNPROFOR should be resolved through negotiations." So my question is this: Have you had occasion to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right that VKRS is, in fact -- stands for Supreme Command of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that Major-General Milan Gvero who signed this document sent this document, in fact, on behalf of the Supreme Command, informing thereby the units that are mentioned here as the addressees; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on Bosnian Serb military communications. That's why understanding. That's my understanding of the document, but I can't attest to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the key issue here is this: Did you at any point in time receive information that at a meeting between Mr. De Mello and General Soubirou, Mr. Akashi and Karadzic, there was an agreement reached that VRS soldiers in the stated sectors should change into civilian clothes as stated here in this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I accompanied Mr. De Mello from Sarajevo to Gorazde after the agreement was reached between Mr. Akashi and Dr. Karadzic. I was -- Mr. De Mello was the head of civil affairs for UNPROFOR based in Zagreb but sent by Mr. Akashi to help resolve the Gorazde crisis. Mr. De Mello was a senior official and led the first convoy of UNPROFOR from Sarajevo to Gorazde following the agreement. And so I was present there at the time and this issue of Serb forces remaining within the 3-kilometre total exclusion zone was a source of disagreement between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serb authorities, and what was agreed from the UNPROFOR side, what we had understood and agreed to, was that as per the agreement between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Akashi, all Serb forces were required to depart the 3-kilometre total exclusion zone. If there were individuals who were from within that region, primarily on the right bank of the Drina, Serb individuals who had served in the military or had served in the police, and they wished to stay behind as civilians, then they were free to do so as long as they did not wear their military or police uniform and did not carry their weapon. They were not allowed to stay behind as members of formed military police unit just changing their clothes. And I think there was a disagreement between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serbs on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, knowing the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska, that those soldiers were, in fact, from the areas near Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I cannot attest to that one way or the other. I don't have knowledge of that. I'm sorry. I think it's quite likely some were -- almost certainly some were. Whether all were or not, I cannot attest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you are looking at the clock, Mr. Stojanovic. Is this to introduce your last question, or whether you thought it was the right time for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I do have one additional document. I'll be very brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 1D00717. 717.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see this document before us now. I don't know if you've seen it before, sir. The date is the 16th of April, 1994, in other words at the time of the Gorazde crisis. It was issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska signed by General-Colonel Ratko Mladic and entitled: Treatment of civil and prisoners -- civilians and prisoners of war in Gorazde. And it says: "I strictly forbid the mistreatment and physical liquidation of prisoners of war, civilians, and members of international organisations." Under 2: "All commands and members of the VRS are duty-bound to isolate and protect the civilian population in Gorazde by transferring them to more adequate locations." And under 5: "Destruction of movable and immovable property on the liberated territory by torching or destroying is prohibited." So I'm asking you this: According to what you knew, was this order issued by General Mladic implemented? Was it complied with in view of the events in and around Gorazde in those days? And as far as you can remember, were there any actions that ran counter to this order?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: If I can just have a minute to review the text, please, because I've not seen this document before. According to my recollection I have not seen it. It is my experience that this order was not fully implemented by Bosnian Serb military units in and around Gorazde at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then after the break I will ask you how that portion of this order not being complied with actually expressed itself in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- we had one on the screen before, Mr. Stojanovic. We did not even have time to look at it because you had -- you had already changed it for another one. Would you consider during the break with the precise 65 ter numbers which other ones you would also wish to tender. But for this one at this moment, Madam Registrar ... ? Let's first finish this one. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. Document 1D717 receives number D187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D187 is admitted into evidence. I'd like to take the break now. Mr. Stojanovic, if you would put down on a little piece of paper which of the others you want to tender, then we can deal with it far more quickly after the break. The witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
