utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just inform the Chamber -- I know that we had some discussions earlier in the week about possible need to sit extra time in order to complete the witnesses. I've spoken to Mr. Stojanovic. It appears that there will be no need for any extra time. He's confident that he can complete his examination in the regular hearing time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I am looking at how we finished yesterday, the Chamber already thought that there would be no need, although it was not confirmed, it was mainly introduced through the previous witness who I think concluded his testimony well in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to suggest that the document dated the 27th of April, 1994, be tendered -- be admitted into evidence. I commented on it and discussed it with the witness. 1D708 is the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D708 receives number D188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D188 is admitted. Any other document, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No, Your Honour. There will be other ones, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's also nothing about 65 ter 09738? You don't want to tender that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you remember we -- you were saying that before the break that as far as you know General Mladic's order dated the 16th of April, 1994, wasn't fully respected. Do you remember in what respect the order was not fully respected? Who failed to abide by the order and where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have it on our screen again so that we can follow the comments of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 1D717.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the screen already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D187 is the number now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. The timing there of the -- this order of 16 April 1994 was right in the middle of the crisis, so of course things that happened before the 16th of April cannot have fallen under this order but -- and there were many problems before the 16th. Nonetheless, even afterward there was, for instance, I believe significant destruction of property. For instance, when I accompanied that first convoy led by Mr. De Mello, UNPROFOR convoy, from Sarajevo to Gorazde, as we approached Gorazde very late at night, around midnight, I saw many homes burning still -- on fire at the time, other homes destroyed, though it's possible that some of those destroyed homes could have been destroyed before April 16th, but certainly the ones that were on fire were contemporaneously destroyed. A number of dead animal carcasses. So I think there was destruction of property in and around Gorazde following 16 April. There was also an UNPROFOR soldier killed in the Gorazde area. There -- excuse me one second. The treatment of civilians at -- following April 16th -- and there certainly was not adequate humanitarian assistance brought in to them by the United Nations because of impediments imposed by the Bosnian Serb military. So I think both in the letter and in the spirit of this order there were some significant violations following April 16th by the Bosnian Serb forces in and around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we briefly go through a few of them. The first one is the prohibition of cruel treatment, as well as the abuse and physical destruction of the civilian population. Did you see any violation of that order or was that included in the previous part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that first part, Your Honour, involved a number of different concepts. Cruel treatment, abuse and physical destruction of civilian population, prisoners of war, and members of international organisations, but trying to interpret it as literally as possible the way it's written, the -- physical destruction of civilian population, no, I don't believe I could say I personally -- other than the fact that the population of Gorazde was -- was imprisoned as a whole and given very limited access to -- to humanitarian assistance. There was a military assault on the enclave which involved or included destruction of or shelling of the area that led to civilian deaths. I guess that may fall within that, but that's only thing that I could say on the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second category, that is, isolation and protection of the civil population by transferring them to more adequate localities. Was that done and do you have any understanding of what the basis of this order was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the civilian population was not isolated, although I don't think the Bosnian Serb authorities or military could have isolated the civilian population in Gorazde from the military population. It was a small enclave; things were intermixed. But there were not transfers of the population that -- that I'm aware of at that time. And I don't know what exactly the intention of that part of the order in paragraph 2 refers to. It could refer to different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, abuse of prisoners of war, and, 3, any knowledge about that whether that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4: "All members of the international organisations to be sheltered on the territory of the Republika Srpska and to be accommodated and secure treatment in accordance with their mandate."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this two comments, Your Honour. One, there was the killing of the UNPROFOR soldier. Putting aside the shooting down of the NATO jet, but the killing of the UNPROFOR soldier is one specific example where that part of the order was not respected. But more broadly the last part of that paragraph, "secure treatment in accordance with their mandate," certainly we were not accorded the treatment we needed in accordance with our mandate, i.e., freedom of movement, ability to operate to move freely in and around -- to Gorazde and then within the Gorazde area. We could not freely move our personnel there from, say, Sarajevo. Once there, we could not move freely about and we could not deliver the humanitarian assistance that was required. So I believe that part was clearly not followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I follow you, the -- perhaps the order was followed but was -- to the extent that -- but that it was not in accordance with your mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I meant to refer to at the last part of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comment on the destruction of movable and immovable property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in addition to my previous answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Anything about confiscated MTS, materiel technical resources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't have any personal knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you the following: As far as you know, was that Sea Harrier plane destroyed before this order was issued by General Mladic, and was this something that occurred subsequent to this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was right around that time. It may have been before but it was right around that time. I don't know. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may sit down, Mr. Mladic. If there's any need to consult -- Mr. Stojanovic, for urgent consultation 30 seconds at a low voice is allowed; otherwise, you would have to wait until the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Please be seated, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a few other questions that relate to this crisis in Gorazde to put to you. Would you agree that in this conflict in Gorazde -- or rather, this conflict in Gorazde was preceded by numerous incidents from the Gorazde safe haven incidents that were launched against Serbian villages, surrounding Serbian places, or rather, provocations that were launched against these places?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: As I mentioned previously, I only arrived on April 9th when perhaps those incidents to the extent they occurred had already occurred. So I do not have personal knowledge of that. I did hear reports or complaints from the Bosnian Serb authorities of such incidents, but I have no direct personal knowledge. And the UNPROFOR reporting on such incidents to a large extent took place before my arrival; and in addition, our ability to report on such incidents was limited because of the restrictions on our freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of personally learning about the contents of the warehouse of the former JNA warehouse in the suburb of Gorazde, Kopaci, this was under ground. What sort of logistics, what sort of equipment, what sort of resources were kept there? Did you find anything out about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the pilot of the downed plane was an English pilot?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly my understanding. It was a British aircraft piloted by a British pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the UNPROFOR member who was killed, was he part of an UNPROFOR mission or was he, in fact, guiding NATO planes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, there were two British officers killed or British personnel killed in Gorazde, both of whom were UNPROFOR personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And was their mission to guide the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. I should say, however, if that was their mission it's quite likely that I would not be aware of that because of the nature of those kinds of military operations. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Because that is a question that we also put to generals who have already appeared here. Would you agree with me that the bullet that killed these UNPROFOR members is -- or the bullet fired by the UNPROFOR members is in dispute. There is no agreement as to who fired that bullet that killed the UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It is my understanding that UNPROFOR had concluded that the shot was fired from Bosnian Serb-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now have a look at a document. It's a 65 ter document, 18775. We'll have a look at it in the e-court. Unfortunately we only have it in English, Your Honours. And we'll focus on paragraph 3 in this document. It's a telegram of the 25th of April, 1994, sent by Mr. de Lapresle to Mr. Annan. In paragraph 3 it states the following: "The situation on the ground in Gorazde is much improved. The Army of Republika Srpska has withdrawn 3 kilometres from the line agreed on by Karadzic and Akashi." And it further states that the BiH is of no assistance because snipers, their snipers, opened fire on the Serbs who were withdrawing from those lines, at least 13 BSA casualties resulted in the direction of Ustipraca. Do you remember this document? Have you already seen it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I do not remember it and it's very unlikely that I would have seen it at the time as this code cable was generated in Zagreb and I was at the time based in Sarajevo and I think on that day I was already in Gorazde. So we would not have had access to these code cables in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed of such a situation at any point in time? Were you provided with such information according to which ABiH members at the time of the withdrawal of the Republika Srpska army, according to the Karadzic-Akashi agreement, opened fire on members of the Republika Srpska army and opened fire from sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I would have been informed of most significant military or operational developments in respect to the Gorazde crisis, including such an incident as this which I would have and we would have characterised as very serious. Although I do not recollect at this time the specific incident, that just simply may be due to the passage of time and I don't dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this, in fact, happened, would that have meant that the ABiH had violated the Karadzic-Akashi agreement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I would have to review the specific terms of the agreement and also need to have more information about this specific incident, but it's -- that's certainly a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that according to the information you had and on the basis of your experience, according to the information you had while present in the field, the ABiH was operating in the Gorazde safe haven and that army was armed and functioned like a standard military unit in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It was certainly my understanding that there were elements of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina present in Gorazde and they were trying to function as a military force. I don't know that they were operating as a standard military force because of the unique situation in -- present in Gorazde. Basically they were isolated, surrounded by their opposing force, their enemy, and as a result they had to operate in a quite different way. And I think their -- the resources available to them, their logistics, for instance, were a significant problem. But certainly I agree that there were elements of the Bosnian government military forces in Gorazde acting in a military way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in relation to this. Were there any international legal instruments, Security Council Resolutions, other agreements which were valid agreements that would prevent them from having their presence in Gorazde and to act as a military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to my understanding and recollection, there were no legal requirements created by the Security Council or agreements entered into by the parties that would have required the Bosnian military to withdraw from the safe areas, including Gorazde, or to limit their activities in the Gorazde safe area to the point where they -- they did not act as a military force according to my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. It seems that Mr. Mladic would like to hand out a note. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'll go back to the issue we were dealing with, that concerns the safe havens. According to your understanding and according to your understanding of the safe havens, would it be legitimate if there was an attack launched by the ABiH? If there were certain formations in the safe haven, would it be legitimate in the case of such attack for the Republika Srpska army to respond to the attack launched?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This was an issue of constant -- that created constant difficulties for UNPROFOR and relates to the previous discussion on clarification of the safe area concept. Because according to my understanding, the legal obligations created by UN Security Council Resolutions 824 and 836 were -- imposed very significant constraints on the Bosnian Serb -- constraints and obligations on the Bosnian Serb army in terms of not attacking the safe areas and withdrawing to a safe distance from the safe areas. But those resolutions did not make similar or associated demands or create obligations on the Bosnian government forces so that from a legal perspective the Bosnian government forces could launch attacks from the safe areas. And if they did so, the Bosnian Serb army was prohibited from responding. As a legal matter, according to Security Council Resolutions and hence the UNPROFOR mandate, whether that was fair or just or wise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is exceptionally that -- first the witness cannot be interrupted in answering a question so you should -- Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking. Is there a problem with the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he has a problem with receiving the interpretation again. That is my understanding of the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be resolved then. We'll wait until it has been resolved. I'll speak a few words and see whether Mr. Mladic receives interpretation. Do you now receive interpretation? One second. Usually on channel 6. We will wait until the technicians have resolved the problem. That is, Mr. Mladic, there is no need to speak about it. It will be resolved and we will stop until it has been resolved. Is it a technical problem or is it a choice of the channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I check at this moment whether Mr. Mladic now hears what I say in a language he understands?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am receiving the interpretation now, but I would like everything that I did not hear to be interpreted for my benefit again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, for the next break, I don't know for how long it was, we could ask Madam Registrar to make a print-out of, well let's say the last two pages from before Mr. Mladic told us that he had problems and then you have an opportunity to go through that with the assistance of whomever because we have only the English transcript at this moment. But you'll find a solution for that I take it. Meanwhile, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll put another question to you that concerns Gorazde now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first allow the witness to complete his answer to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought he had completed his answer. He repeated what his position was, the one that he expressed in the course of the previous session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I was just about to conclude my answer, but I think the substantive point had been made. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then time for the next question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As instructed by General Mladic, I would like to ask you whether you knew that within the Gorazde safe area there was a special purposes factory for producing military ammunition and the name was Pobide [phoen] Gorazde and there was also a chemical industry plant, a Zotare [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I had heard reports of the Bosnian forces in Gorazde making somehow their own munitions. I have no direct knowledge of such a factory. I haven't, for instance, seen it with my eyes, but I did hear reports. I don't know the name of that factory. I had not heard of a factory manufacturing chemicals in Gorazde or the name of that factory either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If what you heard was correct, given your understanding - and I'm referring to your understanding - of the term "safe area," would this have represented a violation of the concept of a state -- of a safe area in accordance with international law. Would that have been the case if ammunition was being produced in such an area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you're referring to the concept of a safe area in international law, you are hereby invited to tell us exactly what you're referring to. Is this an agreed safe area between the parties with -- or is it a concept which was used, for example, in Security Council Resolutions 824 and 836. We should clearly distinguish what we are dealing with at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, preparing for this I read both resolutions of the Security Council a number of times because for years I have been dealing with the Srebrenica story. The resolution itself is open to interpretation and that is the problem that the witness today has spoken about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the only thing I'm inviting you to do is are you asking whether it was in violation of the safe areas as defined in the Security Council Resolutions or by any other definition. Then the witness has a clear point of reference for his answer. If there would be present such factories, would that violate the safe area as outlined in the Security Council Resolutions 824 and 836? That is now the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, such a presence of a munitions factory in the safe area would not, according to my understanding, violate either Resolutions 824, 836, or other Security Council Resolutions related to the Bosnian conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's precisely what I was hoping to elicit, the interpretation of this witness. Now, Your Honour, I would like to tender 65 ter 18775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18775 receives number D189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you would agree, I take it, that it would be MFI'd until you have provided the B/C/S translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We did not receive interpretation of your words. Could you please repeat what you just said, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. This would be my proposal. I would like to tender this document with an MFI identification pending the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D189 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now briefly let's focus on paragraph 27 of your statement. Let me say that that's P874, document P874, and in this paragraph you talk about a crisis situation dealing with the release of an UNPROFOR official. If you recall, a number of documents are mentioned here and briefly I will tell you, or rather, I'd like to show you paragraph 27, the portion specifically which says that Mr. Andreev had met with Mr. Karadzic on the 31st of May, 1994, and that Karadzic indicated on that occasion that the said gentleman would be released once the Serbs had received written confirmation of his status as an UNPROFOR staff member and assurances that his mistake would not be repeated. Very briefly, could you agree with me that this incident occurred when it was established that there were individuals in the vehicle of this UNPROFOR member who were not properly accredited and who had on them over 300.000 Deutschemarks, were taking the money into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I am familiar with the incident. I do not recall the amount of money that was supposedly found in the vehicle, though I have no reason to question the amount you cited. What is important about this incident and an issue embedded in your question about whether the people were properly accredited, and here there was a fundamental difference of opinion between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serb authorities on our rights to transport people, to move our own people, transport other people, transport goods for our operation. And all too often the Bosnian Serb authorities, the military authorities at check-points, would stop UNPROFOR, take people out of our vehicles and imprison them, take goods, confiscate goods, from us. And this was a serious violation of the obligations of the Bosnian Serb authorities as created by Security Council Resolutions to give us unimpeded freedom of movement. And it was a source of constant impediment to the conduct of our operations. And this is just one such incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular incident it was established that one of the people who were in the vehicle of an UNPROFOR member asked the UNPROFOR member to get in his vehicle and go through the check-point and bring 300.000 Deutschemarks into Sarajevo. So this fact, this particular fact and this particular case, is this fact correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I don't know if it's correct. If it is correct then that UNPROFOR staff member made a mistake or did something wrong that he should not have done. However, the response to that -- and I know this from my experience then and my current position, the response to that is for the authority concerned - in this case the Bosnian Serb authority - to bring that issue to the attention of the proper UNPROFOR authorities and for us to take action. It does not give the Bosnian Serbs any right whatsoever to stop a UN vehicle, take people out of a UN vehicle, to search a UN vehicle, to take goods out of a UN vehicle. And in this case and in many others, I believe the Bosnian Serb military were in flagrant violation of UN privileges and immunities and their responsibilities to us under international law and Security Council Resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this UNPROFOR member released the following day?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: He was soon thereafter released. It's quite likely the following day, but I can't say for certain it was that day. But yes, he was very soon released.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this 65 ter document, 10650, or rather, a set of documents as placed on the 65 ter list by the OTP. The entire batch of documents deals with this particular incident and the entire batch is numbered 10650.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber is quite interested to learn what these documents are. The only thing we know until now is that they are on the Prosecution's list. We haven't seen them. You want us to admit into evidence material which we have even no idea about what they are. If you could briefly describe, for example, what it is that would certainly already assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's a document that was drafted by the witness, the present witness, on the 8th of June, 1994, describing the entire incident. Then there is a letter sent by Mr. Viktor Andreev to Mr. Radovan Karadzic, mentioning -- or rather, this letter was mentioned in the statement, this witness's statement, and the letter deals with the same incident. Then there is a document drafted by the present witness on the 6th of June, 1994, referring to the letter sent by Mr. Viktor Andreev to Professor Koljevic in conjunction with this incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that all to be found in 65 ter 10650 or are you referring to other 65 ter numbers as well? Because there I only see a fax sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, from what I got from the OTP all of these actually comprise a document numbered 10650, a summary of all of these events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that is dealt with in the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps it would be helpful to pull up 10650. The front fax sheet describes that on the 8th of June a series of documents are being faxed. And so the entire -- it's a fax document and the fax itself that explains it is a series of documents relating to this incident that's described in paragraph 27 of the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now at least we know what we are supposed to admit into evidence, Mr. Stojanovic. There is no objection. I take it you want to tender it from the bar table because you have not shown it to the witness, but it relates to a matter about which he has testified and therefore bar tabling this document at this moment would not meet any objection certainly where the Prosecution does not object. We have it on our screen anyhow. We could make it even a real exhibit. Mr. Banbury, do you see the document on your screen at this moment and do you remember that you have drafted it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes to both questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Madam Registrar, the number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10650 receives number D190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D190 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at paragraph 35 of your statement, which statement is now P874. And could we have in e-court 65 ter 09467. Sir, this is a report sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan. It is dated the 14th of July, 1994, and it relates to a meeting between foreign ministers of Great Britain and France, Douglas Hurd and Alain Juppe, with the warring parties. And I would just like to ask you a few things here. Could we focus on paragraph 3 of this document, summarising the talks between Minister Douglas Hurd with the leading men of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation. I assume that you drafted this document as it is stated here; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, though I should clarify that the covering code cable, the document that was shown or the page shown just before this, is a cover sheet or covering code cable that UNPROFOR headquarters attached to the report and sent to UN headquarters in New York. So I did not draft that first page that was there; however, that page just attaches the report that I did draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question related to paragraph 3 of this document. That is your text; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, the whole report, I believe, is my text except the covering code cable, including paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just briefly hear this: Minister Hurd in his conversation with Federation representatives, or more specifically Mr. Izetbegovic, asked whether it was possible for Serbs in Bosnia to enter into confederation with the FRY as has already been done with Croatia? And the second question, whether he saw a possibility where the eastern enclaves would be exchanged for other territory and Izetbegovic gave a negative question to both questions and pointed out one thing and that's what I want to ask you about. The only possibility for any special ties to be established between the Bosnian Serbs and Serbia, according to him, would be if the same ties were established between the Bosnian government and the Muslims in Sandzak. In response to the second question, Izetbegovic stated that he did not believe in exchange of territory. So my question is this: Where is Sandzak, that area that is mentioned here in your -- in this summary of yours?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It's in the Federal Republic of -- at the time the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that position of Mr. Izetbegovic's pointed out for the first time to you or was it something that you were aware of from some of his earlier speeches or talks or discussion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't recall that he said anything of that sort or you don't recall that he had said something like that before this meeting with Mr. Hurd?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I had heard him state that position either personally or through the press before this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in paragraph 5 of this summary that you drafted and the same talks -- could we move on to the next page in both versions, both B/C/S and English for paragraph 5. It says here that Mr. Hurd had said to Mr. Izetbegovic that it was necessary to recognise the realities, including the fact that it was impossible for Bosnian Serbs to sever all ties with Serbia because such ties would inescapably still exist. And then Hurd said that although he would not inform Serbs of this, it was necessary for Bosnians to understand that NATO would not wage their war. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what this is a reference to? First of all, why was it his view that he should not or why did he say that he wouldn't inform the Serbs of this request put forth by Izetbegovic or his position? And second, why did he warn Bosnians that NATO would not wage their war?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The role of NATO in the Bosnian conflict, particularly from, I would say, February 1994 with some decisions of the North Atlantic Council and going forward was a source of great contention, in capitals, around the world and certainly in Bosnia. And there was a -- I think a hope -- a strong hope on the part of the Bosnian government that NATO would become an ally of theirs in their war, in their conflict with the Bosnian Serbs. They wanted that for, I believe, political as well as military reasons. And they, I think, sought to achieve that objective or convince politicians to have NATO fight on their side. On the other hand, I think the Bosnian Serbs were very fearful of NATO entering the war against them. So here the foreign secretary of one of the Permanent Members of the Security Council and a NATO member is conveying at least his position or the position of the United Kingdom on what the role of NATO was. Now, the reason -- I'm speculating here, I don't know if you want me to do that, but to answer your question about why he would have said to President Izetbegovic that -- what Mr. Hurd would have said to President Izetbegovic that he would not tell the Bosnian Serbs this is because he thought the threat of NATO military action was a source of powerful leverage in negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs. And if that threat were either diminished or removed, then the leverage that the international community had over the Bosnian Serbs, trying to get them to agree to peace or whatever, would be correspondingly diminished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doesn't it seem, sir, that whenever discussions dealing with certain proposals for a peace agreement were being in the phase of being concluded, the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina would always come up with new demands from the other warring parties including, in this case, where the Contact Group was being discussed when they came up with this request to have special ties with a portion of another -- or the population of another part of the former Yugoslavia, the part of the territory which is part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's approximately 17 questions in one, Mr. Stojanovic. I would not mind if you would focus on certain aspects of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me simplify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your experience that whenever there were negotiations between the warring parties while you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were always new demands being put forward, demands on the other warring party that would then delay the signing of a peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Both sides routinely tried to - as is absolutely normal and expected - to maximise their position in negotiations and get international support for their position. I do think there was a regular pattern where once negotiations had concluded or the international community in the form of a Contact Group proposal or other peace plans, once the international community had put a proposal on the table, the Bosnian government would kind of complain and push and try and maximise their position up to the point where the proposal was put on the table or finalised. But then they would -- because there were certain fundamental principles always embedded in those proposals, the Bosnian government would try and lock in those positions. I don't think they tried to change the -- their demands at that time. What they tried to do, I think, was lock in the elements of the proposal that they found absolutely critical, like territorial integrity, and that put the Bosnian Serbs in a very difficult position because those international proposals invariably contained elements that the Bosnian Serbs were not willing to accept, thus the demands that were -- thus it was much more often the case that it was the Bosnian Serbs putting additional demands on the table at that stage in a negotiation than it was the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. I think we should take a break. The witness may follow the usher. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I put the following on the record. At the end of the session of last Friday, the 1st of February, the Chamber admitted into evidence Rule 65 ter number 22565E as Exhibit P841 through Martin Bell as a witness. It should be clarified that like the other video-clips tendered by the Prosecution through this witness, Exhibit P841 should have been MFI'd pending verification of the accuracy of the transcript by CLSS; and therefore, the status of P841 is now that it is MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember we were looking at a document that you drafted after the meeting of the Ministers Hurd and Juppe with the warring parties. And I would just like to deal with item 5 where you commented on the words used by Mr. Hurd. He said that it was important for the Bosnians to understand that NATO wouldn't be waging war on their behalf. In the course of your stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you have the opportunity of seeing or learning about the basis on which the Bosnia and Herzegovinian leadership drew the conclusion that NATO might wage their war, so to speak, wage a war for them?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I, on many occasions, heard different members of the Bosnian government leadership talk about what they thought the role of NATO ought to be. I assessed it to be more of an aspiration of what NATO should do than a conclusion that it is what NATO would do. I think they always felt that they were deeply wronged as a victim of the conflict and that the UN and NATO and the world should do more to assist them. And they very much wanted, aspired, to have NATO enter the conflict on their side. Whether they concluded NATO would do that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll conclude with this document now by putting a question to you that relates to paragraph 8. After the meeting with the leaders of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, two ministers left for Pale. They spoke with -- the two ministers went to Pale, spoke to Mr. Karadzic. And if I have understood you correctly in paragraph 8 -- thank you, I think that's the right passage. In that passage you stated that on that occasion Karadzic told the two ministers that it was essential for Republika Srpska to have some form of international identity, international legal identity. In the course of such conversations with these very important leaders, very important countries that were part of the Contact Group, was there a platform of any kind that was expressed in July of 1994 about the sort of international entity, legal international entity, that would be found satisfactory by the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please repeat the question. I'm not sure I understood it precisely. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be briefer. On that occasion, did the leadership of the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina mention the sort of legal personality that Republika Srpska should have, the sort of international legal personality that the Republika Srpska should have in order for them to be satisfied?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I -- I don't know or I do not recall to what detail they went into in that meeting, but it is my general recollection that in this meeting as well as in other contexts in terms of legal personality for the Republika Srpska, the leaders sought to have two main -- they had two main objectives, one - and it's reflected in this paragraph - that they did not want to be legally part of the same entity or state as the Bosnian government or the Bosniak authorities; and two, they wanted the ability to make independent decisions such as confederation with Serbia that they could make on their own without any reference to other authorities such as Sarajevo. Those were -- my -- that was my understanding of their two main objectives certainly in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would this correspond to what was accepted towards the end of 1995 in the Dayton Agreement? Would it correspond to what was granted to Republika Srpska at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think there are important differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to these differences, did Republika Srpska receive more concessions pursuant to the Dayton Agreement than had been asked for by Mr. Karadzic or did they in fact receive fewer concessions than in that agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it gives the Chamber the impression that you are trying to, first of all, make the focus of this case all kinds of negotiations, not to say that they're entirely irrelevant, but they're certainly not the core of this case, and even less whether finally at the very end the parties got what they wished or did not get what they wished, which in itself, of course - and I take it that that is your suggestion, it is about how reasonable it was or not - that would require an analysis which goes far beyond what is relevant in this case. Would you please keep this in mind when continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could answer that question; if not, we will move on.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The arrangements contained in the Dayton Accord provided the Republika Srpska with less than what Dr. Karadzic stated was their objective in the meeting with two foreign ministers. In respect of legal personality, that's all we're talking about here, of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll now conclude with this document. Could you please have a look at paragraph 11. It's in the same document. It says at the press conference following the meeting, the comments made by the Serbs and by Karadzic in particular were of a calmer kind and did not convey the substance of the discussions that had just taken place. Do you have an explanation, a brief explanation for which the substance of these discussions was not conveyed at the press conference?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It was very often the case that discussions inside a private meeting were very complex and involved a wide range of related matters that were hard for people to understand and very hard to convey in a simple manner to journalists. So it's quite natural, I think, in talking to the press that what is said there is much, much, much less than what's said in the meeting. Additionally, positions that are staked out privately in a meeting, there are many good reasons why an official may not want to reflect those publicly to the press, either for the consumption of their public and stakeholders and for the parties on the other side. So I think this was a fairly routine tactic used by many officials on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now have a look at 65 ter document 08149 in e-court. And, sir, I would like to ask you to focus on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it your intention to tender this document which we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I don't think that's necessary. We would only be encumbering the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Stojanovic, often a reference was made to what was found in a certain paragraph which was not read out in its entirety, so therefore I would suggest that you do tender it. I mean, a reference was made in this paragraph; how do you interpret this? Then of course the Chamber should have the whole of the paragraph in evidence to evaluate the evidence. So you tender it. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09467 receives number D191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D191 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The document you mention in paragraphs 41 and 42 of your statement is something I would like us to comment on. Because here you also speak about the presence of General Mladic. Can we clear up something. When was this meeting, in fact, held? Because in your statement in paragraph 41 it says on the 21st of July, 1994. And if I read through your report it seems it's the 21st of June, sent on the 22nd of June. What is, in fact, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I read the date of the document as 22 July, the subject indicating the meeting took place on the 21st of July. And in the opening sentence it says, "I," meaning Viktor Andreev, "met yesterday in Jahorina ..." et cetera, thus referring to -- since the date of the document is the 22nd of July, referring to the 21st of July. So it's my understanding this meeting occurred on the 21st of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see the point -- I see the point --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the translation it reads 22nd of 6th of 1994. So there is apparently -- there is a translation error. The original is clear on the matter; therefore, the translation should be corrected. Could the Prosecution take care -- it's a Prosecution exhibit -- not an exhibit yet, but 65 ter - that you provide a verified translation with the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. And actually, I think this has been admitted as P764, but we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, need to have the accurate date on it. Now, Mr. Stojanovic, if you ask these kind of questions, I would have a look at the original as well, isn't it? Someone will be able to read it and then we can avoid that we have to unnecessary spend time on it. Then you give a call to the Prosecution and inform them that the translation is wrong and we don't have to spend time on it. That's the appropriate way of dealing with these kind of matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 2 of this summary, this message that was sent, I assume that you are the author of this message as it says here. In paragraph 2 it says that General Rose lodged a protest because fire was opened on three UN planes in the previous 24 hours. As far as you remember General Galic informed them that fire had been opened from a building located on the Muslim side. And this information hadn't been verified. My question is after this meeting and having drafted this report, was this piece of information, in fact, confirmed or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that case I would ask you to have a look at 3(c) in which prisoners of war are referred to. The words spoken by General Mladic are mentioned. In inverted commas he said that: "'... the Serbs cannot forgive international organisations for not honouring the agreement to get the prisoners released.'" That's a quote. What sort of prisoner of war is General Mladic speaking about, could you tell us for the benefit of the Chamber, and what sort of agreement on releasing of prisoners is concerned in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: There were on a consistent basis prisoners of war held by each side and prisoners of war refer to military personnel captured by one side, military personnel of the other side, and not to civilians who by definition are prisoners of war. The agreement that is referred to here was, if I recall correctly, an agreement between the Bosnian Serb authorities and the Bosnian government authorities containing provisions for release by both sides of different prisoners of war. There may have been some requirement on release of -- or provision of information on missing personnel, which was often a contentious issue. What is, I think, significant about this phrase that you've read in this paragraph is that there was an expectation by General Mladic that there was an obligation by UNPROFOR to fulfil the obligations entered into by the Bosnian government. And this was often the case where General Mladic and others would blame UNPROFOR for the actions or lack of actions by the Bosnian government side. And of course it was not -- there was not a legal obligation on UNPROFOR in these agreements to, for instance, release Bosnian prisoners held by the Bosnian government authorities. We were a facilitator. We tried to help. We tried to conclude negotiations. But we did not take on these kinds of obligations. These were obligations by the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, where -- and that's how we find it in the transcript, that's how I heard it, where you said "not to civilians who by definition are prisoners of war," I take it that you misspoke and you would say that they are by definition not prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I thought I said by definition are not prisoners of war. If I misspoke, I apologise, but certainly that is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we now have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And another clarification in line 19, page 78, you said: "There was not a legal obligation on UNPROFOR in these agreements to, for instance, release Bosnian prisoners held by the Bosnian government authorities." I take it that you meant Bosnian Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, if I misspoke, I apologise and that is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic here specifically made a reference to Gorazde and Tarcin prisoners or detainees. Did you have -- or any information about prisoners still being held in Gorazde at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No, not really, just of a general nature. I was aware that the Bosnian government was holding prisoners, but other than that nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mention that General Mladic had also mentioned Tarcin in this part of the text. Could you tell us where Tarcin is, if you know, and do you know how many prisoners and detainees, civilians, were held there under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I am not very familiar with the Tarcin problem. If I recall correctly, this was an issue that predated my arrival in Bosnia but was one that frequently was brought up by the Bosnian Serbs and it's one where very little, if any, progress was achieved over a long time. So I'm just very generally aware that it was an issue, it was there, but I never became quite familiar with the details of the Tarcin issue and prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the silo camp in Tarcin where Serb civilians were held, "silos" in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I heard reports or talk of it. I never personally witnessed or visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to subparagraph (d), 3(d), where you again quote General Mladic as saying that the Serbs were very worried over the rearmament that the Federation armies were undertaking with the co-operation of foreign countries. Was this statement of his according to your information correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: If the question is -- I'm sorry, are you asking me if I understood the Federation was being rearmed? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the question is not clear because the quote given contains a few statements. First, is it true that the Serbs are very worried about the rearmament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding that, yes, indeed, they were concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Second, was the Federation acting in co-operation with foreign countries in the context of rearming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my understanding, based largely on press reports, yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm also looking at the clock. It's quarter past 2.00. Mr. Banbury, we'll adjourn for the day. We'll ask Mr. Stojanovic in a second to tell us whether he's still on schedule and whether he expects -- when he expects to conclude his cross-examination, which might be interesting for you to know as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that is the case and that we will complete our cross-examination within the regular hours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then of course there might be a need for re-examination. How much time do you think you would still need? I mean, if you say, I need tomorrow's session minus 45 minutes, then I think there would be no problem in concluding the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's your expectation that we'll conclude -- that the examination will be concluded in such time that there will be sufficient time left for -- if there's any need for re-examination and questions by the Judges. That is understood which opens a good perspective, Mr. Banbury, to be released tomorrow at the end of tomorrow's session. I would like to instruct you not to speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher and we'll like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- yes. To the extent there may be any confusion about P00764, whether it was admitted or MFI'd, Madam Registrar informs me that it was MFI'd and not yet admitted. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 8th of February at 9.30 in the morning, but I see in Courtroom I, so I misled the witness. We'll resume in Courtroom I and the Victims and Witnesses Section is invited to make the witness aware of the change of courtroom. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
